examples.question_text: Use the double angle formulae to express (a) $\sin^{2}6x$ in terms of $\cos 12x$ and (b) $\cos^{2}\dfrac{x}{6}$ in terms of $\cos\dfrac{x}{3}$.

examples.solution_text:
Square the coefficient as well: $(4\cos 3x)^{2}=16\cos^{2}3x$. Use $\cos^{2}3x=\dfrac{1+\cos 6x}{2}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(4\cos 3x)^{2}\,dx\\&=8\int_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(1+\cos 6x)\,dx\\&=8\left[x+\dfrac{\sin 6x}{6}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{12}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\\&=8\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}+\dfrac{\sin\pi}{6}-\dfrac{\pi}{12}-\dfrac{\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}{6}\right)\\&=8\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}-\dfrac{1}{6}\right)\\&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}-\dfrac{4}{3}\end{aligned}$

coverage.summary: Authored five examples covering all four assessed methods, including fractional frequencies, scalar factors, exact definite integrals and squared-amplitude preparation. Used the booklet's double-angle process throughout. Questions and solutions are separate editable fields; solution prose inherits renderer blue, and continuation working has phantom equals gutters. examples.derivation: Setting A=6x in cos(2A)=1−2sin²(A) gives sin²(6x)=(1−cos(12x))/2. Setting A=x/6 in cos(2A)=2cos²(A)−1 gives cos²(x/6)=(1+cos(x/3))/2. Both rearrangements follow the supplied Review and Foundation Q1–2.

4sin²(3x/4)=2−2cos(3x/2), whose primitive is 2x−(4/3)sin(3x/2)+C. Differentiation returns 2−2cos(3x/2). The fractional frequency and scalar factor retain the booklet's double-angle integration method.
cos²(8x)=(1+cos(16x))/2, so its primitive is x/2+sin(16x)/32+C. Differentiation gives (1+cos(16x))/2. This adapts the supplied cosine-square worked example.

A primitive of sin²(4x) is x/2−sin(8x)/16. At x=π/12 it equals π/24−√3/32 because sin(2π/3)=√3/2; at x=0 it equals zero. The exact difference matches the candidate and follows the supplied sine-square definite-integral example.

(4cos(3x))²=16cos²(3x)=8(1+cos(6x)). Its primitive is 8x+(4/3)sin(6x). The upper value is 4π/3 and the lower value is 2π/3+4/3, giving 2π/3−4/3. Squaring the amplitude is accepted assessment preparation; the integration follows the supplied cosine-square definite tasks.
